catalog_quote: 2.7 Word stress. In basic roots, primary stress is normally applied to the penultimate syllable of a word. Secondary stress applies to every alternate syllable to the left of the penultimate syllable: /ˈga.ni/ 'eat', /βa.ˈtsu.ru/ 'choose', /ˌma.ri.ˈbu.ku/ 'humpback snapper'. Abma is quantity-sensitive. Long vowels take stress, regardless of their position in the word: /ˈβa:.ta/ 'be tight', /ˈe:.naŋ/ 'something, someone', /mwa.ˈte:.te/ 'chicken', /ta.ˈka:/ 'god'. Words ending in closed syllables typically receive word-final stress: /lel.ˈkat/ 'be angry', /sa.ˈdok/ 'sit down', /ha.ˈβin/ 'woman', /me.ˈram/ 'moonlight', /le.ˈleh/ 'bathe', /na.ˈŋih/ 'when'. new_statements.quote: In basic roots, primary stress is normally applied to the penultimate syllable of a word. Secondary stress applies to every alternate syllable to the left of the penultimate syllable: /ˈga.ni/ 'eat', /βa.ˈtsu.ru/ 'choose', /ˌma.ri.ˈbu.ku/ 'humpback snapper'. Abma is quantity-sensitive. Long vowels take stress, regardless of their position in the word: /ˈβa:.ta/ 'be tight', /ta.ˈka:/ 'god'. Words ending in closed syllables typically receive word-final stress: /sa.ˈdok/ 'sit down', /ha.ˈβin/ 'woman'. Where long vowels and closed final syllables both occur in a single word, then long vowels take precedence for the purposes of stress assignment: /ˈha:.pak/ 'child'. Stress marking beyond the basic root word level is a complicated matter and merits a study of its own.

new_statements.relation_note: This direct read confirms verbatim what the catalog already holds: default penult, CVV and final CVC attract stress, CVV outranks CVC, alternating secondaries; nothing new to add beyond the exceptions and hedges already recorded. Note the 'not yet obtained' tag on this work in READALL_TARGETS is stale: the text was downloaded 2026-09-12; only the 156 MB page-image PDF remains unfetched.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default primary stress on the penultimate syllable of a basic root, with secondary stress on every alternate syllable leftward; quantity-sensitive overrides: a long vowel attracts primary stress wherever it stands in the word, and a word ending in a closed syllable typically takes final stress; when both compete, the long vowel wins (CVV > final CVC > default penult). §3.1.2.2 (p.45) restates this as 'long syllables and closed syllables are stressed, regardless of their position in the word' and says affixed roots 'usually' keep penultimate stress, while warning that stress beyond the basic root 'is not straightforward.. More research is necessary'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Stated: 'Secondary stress applies to every alternate syllable to the left of the penultimate syllable', e.g. /ˌma.ri.ˈbu.ku/ 'humpback snapper' (§2.7 p.35); assumed to hold in multimorphemic words too, 'with each alternating syllable to the left also being stressed' (§3.1.2.2 p.45).
new_statements.exceptions: fn.11 p.36: '[i.'be] "where" contradicts the rule that stress occurs in the penultimate syllable' (given a diachronic explanation, /i/ + /be-/ + lost CV possessive). §2.9 p.40: loanwords keep donor-language stress, 'disregarding Abma's internal word stress rules', with a listed handful that nativise ([bo.'tel] 'bottle', [ka.'lib] 'calipers', [os.bi.'tal] 'hospital', [re.'sis.ta.rem] 'register', one pronunciation of 'Saturday' [sa.'re.re]). §3.1.2.2 p.45: [mwa.net.'bo] 'he will lay down' stressed on first and third syllables, 'Why this is so is unclear'. §2.8 p.35: sentence-level stress 'is not yet understood'. Hedges throughout ('normally', 'typically', 'usually maintained').
new_statements.identity_note: The grammar describes the Suru Mwerani (SM) dialect, the largest of Abma's three dialects (SM, Suru Rabwanga/Suru Bo, Suru Kavian), §1.1 p.1 and §1.3 (text-layer lines 209, 289-299); the book uses the name Abma for the language Glottolog lists as Apma (apma1240). No dialect mismatch with the catalog languoid.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement between sources (only one work is listed and it is the source behind the catalog's existing coding). One internal tension inside Schneider 2010: §2.7 (p.35) exemplifies closed-syllable attraction only for word-FINAL closed syllables ('Words ending in closed syllables typically receive word-final stress'), whereas §3.1.2.2 (p.45) generalises to 'long syllables and closed syllables are stressed, regardless of their position in the word'; the examples never show a non-final CVC or a pre-antepenult CVV drawing stress, so the unbounded version is asserted rather than exemplified. The author also flags that stress beyond the basic root and at sentence level is not understood ([mwa.net.'bo] unexplained).

audit.reasoning: The classification (weight-hedged: default penult, long vowel stressed anywhere, final closed syllable attracts stress, CVV > final CVC; secondaries alternate leftward; author hedges beyond the root) rests on the standard and only reference grammar of Abma (Schneider 2010, PL 608, from her 2006 PhD), which we hold as the ANU open text; the deciding quotation is present verbatim at §2.7 p.35 and the supporting passages (§3.1.2.2 p.45, fn.11, §2.8, §2.9) are all present as cited. The hedged quantity-sensitive coding faithfully reflects the author's own caveats ('typically', 'not straightforward', 'merits a study of its own'). Glottolog lists no phonology work; the one open item not yet obtained (Schneider & Gray 2015) was downloaded and is silent on stress; Gray's archived web page is silent; no instrumental or theoretical stress study of Apma surfaced. Nothing found suggests a reclassify.
